title: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY WITH VARIABLE INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES

relationships.phenotype: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY WITH VARIABLE INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the JARID2 gene on chromosome 6p22.3.

checks.claim: Developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the JARID2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: JARID2 (Jumonji, AT Rich Interactive Domain 2; OMIM 601594) haploinsufficiency has been associated with a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome.
checks.explanation: Haploinsufficiency means a heterozygous loss. The paper describes the syndrome but does not use the OMIM name DIDDF, which is standard naming.

checks.claim: The JARID2 gene is located on chromosome 6p22.3.
checks.evidence_quote: We suggest JARID2 and ATXN1, both harbored in 6p22.3, as disease causing genes.

paragraphs.text: JARID2 haploinsufficiency causes a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by developmental delay, cognitive impairment ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, autistic features, and behavioral abnormalities. Dysmorphic facial features include high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and full lips (Verberne et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Barøy et al. (2013) described 4 unrelated patients with de novo deletions in chromosome 6p22.3 that included the JARID2 gene, identified in a cohort of about 3,600 patients ascertained for neurodevelopmental disorders. Patients 1 to 3 (2 girls aged 15 and 6.5 years and a 4-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous Norwegian or Norwegian and English parents) had larger deletions that also included ATXN1, and had moderate, moderate, and severe intellectual disability, respectively. Patient 4, a 6.5-year-old boy born to nonconsanguineous Lebanese parents, had a deletion that included only part of JARID2 and DTNBP1; he had a borderline IQ of 74, delayed language development, early-onset muscular hypotonia, and balance and coordination problems. All 4 patients with JARID2 deletion had gait disturbance and similar facial features, the most characteristic being prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, dark infraorbital circles, and midface hypoplasia. Other features in these patients included bulbous nasal tip, full lips, marked Cupid's bow, prominent or pointed chin, clinodactyly of the fifth fingers, and toe anomalies; dyspraxia was suggested in patients 1 and 4. Behavioral abnormalities included hyperactivity, sleeping difficulties, and poor eye contact, and patient 3 fulfilled criteria for autism spectrum disorder. On inspection of photographs available for 7 of 10 previously reported patients with deletions including JARID2, Barøy et al. (2013) confirmed a similar facial pattern and suggested that JARID2 haploinsufficiency might represent a clinically recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) tabulated the features of 8 individuals with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, including a mother and daughter. All had developmental delay; intellectual functioning ranged from normal (the daughter) and learning difficulties (her mother) to borderline intellectual functioning (IQ 82) and mild or moderate intellectual disability. Autistic features were present in 4, and 2 had a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Facial features included high anterior hairline, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, and full lips. Other anomalies in individual patients included submucous cleft palate and bifid uvula, a small posterior fossa cyst or mega cisterna magna, an arachnoid cyst, cryptorchidism, and kyphoscoliosis.

paragraphs.text: In 5 unrelated patients with de novo deletions (0.1 to 4.8 Mb) in chromosome 6p22.3-p24.1 detected by array CGH, Barøy et al. (2013) defined 2 smallest regions of overlap. SRO I (189 kb), deleted in patients 1 to 4, contained JARID2 and DTNBP1; SRO II (116 kb), deleted in patients 1 to 3 and 5, contained GMPR and ATXN1. The deletion in patient 4 removed exons 3 to 18 of JARID2 and exons 7 to 10 of DTNBP1. JARID2 expression in leukocytes was significantly reduced in patients 1 to 4 compared with controls (p less than or equal to 0.01). Patient 5, whose deletion included only GMPR and part of ATXN1, had mild intellectual disability and behavioral abnormalities but no dysmorphic features or gait disturbance were noted. Barøy et al. (2013) considered a contribution of DTNBP1 haploinsufficiency to the features in their patients unlikely and suggested that the concomitant deletion of ATXN1 and JARID2 likely exacerbated the intellectual disability in patients 1 to 3.

paragraphs.text: Using chromosome microarray analysis, exome sequencing, and GeneMatcher, Verberne et al. (2021) identified deletions or single-nucleotide variants in JARID2 in 16 individuals from 15 families with developmental delay and/or intellectual disability. Several of the variants were predicted to result in haploinsufficiency through nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

They noted a high prevalence of intragenic JARID2 copy number variants and emphasized the importance of exon-level analysis.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) studied 11 individuals with JARID2 variants, 7 of whom had been previously reported. Eight carried pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants: 6 had a deletion of at least 1 exon of JARID2, 1 had a de novo frameshift (c.2866dupG, Glu956GlyfsTer72), and 1 had a de novo splice site variant (c.2731+1G-C). Peripheral blood DNA methylation profiling identified a distinct episignature that separated these 8 patients from controls. Three individuals carried missense variants of uncertain significance (R788Q in 2 unrelated individuals and E644K in 1); their methylation profiles clustered with controls, and Verberne et al. (2022) considered that these missense variants might well be benign.

paragraphs.text: Zahir et al. (2016) had previously found a copy number variant involving only exon 6 of JARID2, which occurred apparently de novo in 7 patients with intellectual disability. Investigation of this variant in 2 cohorts showed that it was benign, with a high population frequency (greater than 14%), although it could nevertheless have a contributory effect.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) identified a DNA methylation episignature in peripheral blood from 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants compared with 56 matched controls. A support vector machine classifier based on 150 selected probes gave scores near 1 for all patients and low scores for controls and for patients with other neurodevelopmental disorders, indicating full sensitivity and specificity, and the signature was added to the EpiSign diagnostic test.

checks.evidence_quote: Peripheral blood DNA methylation profiles from 56 control subjects, 8 patients with (likely) pathogenic JARID2 variants and 3 patients with JARID2 VUSs were analyzed.

paragraphs.text: In a 14-year-old boy (patient 4) with moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and a small posterior fossa cyst or mega cisterna magna, Verberne et al. (2022) reported a de novo heterozygous 1-bp duplication (c.2866dupG, NM_004973.4) in the JARID2 gene, resulting in a frameshift (Glu956GlyfsTer72). The variant was classified as pathogenic. The patient's peripheral blood DNA methylation profile clustered with the JARID2 episignature.

agent.process_note: I read all 5 papers. Two had full text: Barøy 2013 and Verberne 2022. Three were abstract only: Zahir 2016, Verberne 2021 and Cadieux-Dion 2022. JARID2 and heterozygosity come from Verberne 2021 and Verberne 2022, which describe haploinsufficiency, de novo heterozygous 6p22 deletions and heterozygous variants. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I left out the gene MIM number; I took the location (6p22.3) from the papers. Verberne 2021 and Cadieux-Dion 2022 are available only as abstracts, so their individual variants, family details and clinical counts could not be reported. The only point-level variants with exact notation are the two P/LP variants in Verberne 2022 (c.2866dupG and c.2731+1G>C). I did not list the three missense VUSs as causal variants, and I described the exon 6 CNV (Zahir 2016) as benign.
